title: Affordability Will Decide AI Winners in India, Peak XV's Anandan Says
excerpt: In NDTV's Walk The Talk, Rajan Anandan argues homegrown companies building smaller, cost-effective models for real-world use can win at home and compete globally, even as AI reshapes outsourcing and software jobs.
body:
• Peak XV Managing Director Rajan Anandan told NDTV that Indian AI companies have a real opportunity to win the domestic market and potentially become global players, with homegrown foundation models designed for affordability and real-world applications.
  • A surge in investment in data centres and GPUs is helping address India's compute constraints, and Anandan discussed India becoming a global provider of AI compute.
  • For workers in outsourcing and software, his message was direct: people across experience levels must become proficient in AI tools to remain employable.
  • In separate remarks reported on November 3, Anandan said India could see 25 to 30 homegrown AI unicorns by 2030 if startups focus on affordable innovation.

Affordability, not scale alone, will decide who wins the artificial intelligence market in India, Peak XV Partners Managing Director Rajan Anandan has argued in a conversation with NDTV. In the interview, part of NDTV's Walk The Talk series, Anandan said Indian AI companies have a real opportunity to win the domestic market and potentially become global players, rather than remaining only consumers of technology built elsewhere.

Smaller models, lower costs

According to NDTV's account of the conversation, homegrown companies are developing foundation models designed for affordability and real-world applications. Anandan argued that smaller, cost-effective models could give Indian companies an edge over global tech giants, whose largest models are far more expensive to build and run. That is the core of the affordability thesis in the interview's headline: products priced for India's market, built around practical uses, stand a better chance of reaching users at scale.

The same theme has run through Anandan's earlier public remarks. At the IndiaAI Summit in February, reported by Outlook Business, he said affordability remained the biggest constraint in online education, pointing out that only 30 to 50 million students paid for online education in a country with nearly 290 million K-12 learners, and argued that AI could finally make high-quality education accessible at scale.

"Of course, valuations have to be reasonable, you've to have profitability, and consistent execution is what will get rewarded."

That remark, reported by Inshorts on November 3, came as Anandan said India is the "number one IPO market in the world, especially for start-ups" and that a focus on affordable innovation could produce 25 to 30 homegrown AI unicorns by 2030.

Compute is catching up, chips will take longer

Anandan told NDTV that a surge in investment in data centres and GPUs is helping address India's compute constraints, and he discussed India's potential to become a global provider of AI compute, alongside the rise of consumer and enterprise AI startups. He was more cautious on hardware further down the stack, explaining why building a semiconductor ecosystem on the scale of Nvidia will take much longer.

Talent is the other constraint he has flagged before. At the IndiaAI Summit, according to Outlook Business, Anandan said India has barely 200 top AI researchers compared with around 3,000 in the United States and 2,300 in the United Kingdom, and that building 10,000 to 15,000 world-class researchers is what it would take to lead. He added that giving serious researchers access to 2,000 GPUs could significantly accelerate progress.

Jobs will change

The interview also addressed work. In a related Walk The Talk segment, NDTV reported Anandan saying AI will transform hundreds of job roles, including those in outsourcing and software development, and that workers across experience levels must become proficient in AI tools to remain employable, warning that the era of staying in the same role for years is over. He also pointed to emerging opportunities such as forward-deployed engineers, who help large enterprises implement AI technologies, and urged workers to identify and develop the skills the changing job market needs.

What happens next

Anandan's argument leaves Indian founders with a specific test: build models and applications that are affordable enough for India's price-sensitive market, useful enough for real-world adoption, and disciplined enough on valuations, profitability and execution to be rewarded by public markets. Whether that produces the unicorns he described will depend on the compute build-out, the researcher pipeline and how quickly workers and companies adapt to the tools he says are already changing their jobs.
nri_angle: Anandan's affordability and jobs arguments speak directly to Indian-origin founders, investors and tech workers in the US watching India's AI build-out.
